entries.question: In a 100 m race, A beats B by 20 m. If A runs at 10 m/s, what is B's speed?
entries.trick: Ratio of speeds = Ratio of distances covered in the same time = 100 : 80 = 5 : 4.
entries.why: Time for A to finish 100 m = 100 ÷ 10 = 10 seconds. In 10 seconds, B covers 100 − 20 = 80 m. B's speed = 80 ÷ 10 = 8 m/s.
entries.why_others_wrong: 12 m/s incorrectly adds 2 m/s to A's speed; 8.33 m/s uses 100/12; 7.5 m/s comes from dividing 60 by 8.

entries.question: In a 1000 m race, A gives B a head start of 100 m and still wins the race by 50 m. What distance does B cover when A finishes the race?
entries.trick: Distance covered by B = (Total Race Distance − Beat Distance) − Head Start.
entries.why: A covers the full 1000 m. B starts 100 m ahead (at 100 m mark) and finishes 50 m behind the 1000 m mark (at 950 m mark). Actual distance B runs = 950 − 100 = 850 m.
entries.why_others_wrong: 900 m forgets the beat distance (1000 − 100); 950 m is B's position on the track, not the distance B ran; 800 m subtracts 100 twice.

entries.question: In a 500 m race, the ratio of speeds of two contestants A and B is 5 : 4. How much head start should A give to B so that the race ends in a dead heat?
entries.trick: Distance B covers = (B's speed ÷ A's speed) × Race Length. Head start = Race Length − Distance B covers.
entries.why: For a dead heat, both reach the finish line at the exact same time. In the time A runs 500 m, B runs (4/5) × 500 = 400 m. Thus, A must give B a head start of 500 − 400 = 100 m.
entries.why_others_wrong: 125 m calculates (5/4) × 100; 80 m calculates (4/5) × 100; 50 m is an arbitrary guess.

entries.knot_name: Confusing distance covered vs remaining
entries.question: A can run 1 km in 3 min 10 sec and B can run the same distance in 3 min 20 sec. By what distance does A beat B in a 1 km race?
entries.trick: Beat distance = Total Distance × (B's time − A's time) ÷ B's time.
entries.why: Time for A = 190 seconds; Time for B = 200 seconds. B's speed = 1000 ÷ 200 = 5 m/s. When A finishes at 190 s, B has run 5 × 190 = 950 m. Beat distance = 1000 − 950 = 50 m.
entries.why_others_wrong: 950 m is the distance B covered, not the beat distance (confusing distance covered vs remaining); 52.6 m incorrectly divides the 10 s difference by A's time (190 s) instead of B's time (200 s).
entries.knot: Selecting the total distance B ran (950 m) instead of subtracting it from the race length (50 m), or placing A's time in the denominator instead of B's time.
entries.trap_explanation: Mistaking the distance B ran (950 m) as the answer, or dividing the 10-second gap by A's time (10/190 × 1000 = 52.6 m).

entries.knot_name: Wrong ratio direction
entries.question: In a 100 m race, A beats B by 10 m and A beats C by 28 m. In a race of 180 m, by how many meters will B beat C?
entries.trick: Ratio of distances covered by B and C = 90 : 72 = 5 : 4. C's distance when B runs 180 m = 180 × (4/5) = 144 m.
entries.why: When A = 100 m, B = 90 m and C = 72 m. B's speed to C's speed ratio = 90 / 72 = 5 / 4. When B covers 180 m, C covers 180 × (4/5) = 144 m. B beats C by 180 − 144 = 36 m.
entries.why_others_wrong: 32.4 m comes from multiplying the simple difference (18 m) by 1.8; 18 m is the beat distance in a 100 m race of A, not 180 m of B; 45 m uses the inverted ratio 5/4.
entries.knot: Directly taking the difference 28 − 10 = 18 m and scaling linearly, ignoring that B has only run 90 m when beating C by 18 m.
entries.trap_explanation: Subtracting 28 − 10 = 18 m and assuming B beats C by 18 m per 100 m of B's run, forgetting that B covered only 90 m to build an 18 m lead over C.

entries.knot_name: Confusing distance covered vs remaining
entries.question: In a 800 m race, A gives B a start of 40 m and beats him by 20 seconds. If A's speed is 8 m/s, what is B's speed?
entries.trick: B's distance = 800 − 40 = 760 m. B's time = A's time + 20 s = 100 + 20 = 120 s.
entries.why: Time taken by A = 800 ÷ 8 = 100 s. Since B is beaten by 20 s, B takes 100 + 20 = 120 s. Distance covered by B = 800 − 40 = 760 m. B's speed = 760 ÷ 120 = 6.33 m/s.
entries.why_others_wrong: 6.67 m/s uses 800 m for B instead of 760 m (forgetting head start); 9.5 m/s subtracts 20 s from A's time instead of adding; 5.83 m/s uses 700 / 120.
entries.knot: Forgetting to subtract head start from B's total distance, or subtracting time penalty instead of adding it.
entries.trap_explanation: Calculating B's speed as 800 ÷ 120 = 6.67 m/s by forgetting that B only had to run 760 m due to the 40 m head start.

entries.knot_name: Wrong ratio direction
entries.question: In a game of 100 points, A can give B 20 points and C 28 points. How many points can B give C in a game of 100 points?
entries.why: When A = 100, B = 80 and C = 72. B's points : C's points = 80 : 72 = 10 : 9. When B scores 100 points, C scores 100 × (9/10) = 90 points. Thus B can give C 100 − 90 = 10 points.
entries.why_others_wrong: 8 points is the simple difference (28 − 20); 12 and 15 points come from wrong ratio scaling.
entries.knot: Subtracting 28 − 20 = 8 points directly without scaling by B's target score of 100.
entries.trap_explanation: Directly subtracting 28 − 20 = 8 points, failing to realize that B's score of 80 must scale up to 100 points.

entries.knot_name: Wrong ratio direction
entries.question: A and B run a 1200 m circular race starting from the same point at speeds of 18 km/hr and 27 km/hr in the SAME direction. After how much time will they meet for the first time at the starting point?
entries.trick: Time to meet at starting point = LCM of individual lap times: LCM(Track ÷ SpeedA, Track ÷ SpeedB).
entries.why: Speed of A = 18 × (5/18) = 5 m/s → Lap time A = 1200 ÷ 5 = 240 s. Speed of B = 27 × (5/18) = 7.5 m/s → Lap time B = 1200 ÷ 7.5 = 160 s. LCM(240, 160) = 480 seconds.
entries.why_others_wrong: 240 s is A's single lap time; 160 s is B's single lap time; 720 s is 240 × 3.
entries.knot: Confusing meeting anywhere on the track (using relative speed) with meeting specifically at the starting point (LCM of individual lap times).
entries.trap_explanation: Using single lap time of one runner instead of calculating both lap times and taking their LCM.

entries.question: Six friends A, B, C, D, E, F sit around a circular table facing the center. A sits directly opposite to D. If B sits adjacent to A, who sits directly opposite to B?
entries.trick: In a 6-person circular table, opposite positions are separated by 3 seats (180 degrees).
entries.why: With 6 evenly spaced seats (1 to 6), opposite pairs are (1,4), (2,5), and (3,6). If A is at pos 1 and D is at pos 4, B must be at pos 2 (or 6). The seat directly opposite to B (pos 2) is pos 5, which is occupied by E (or F, where E is the corresponding opposite seat).
entries.why_others_wrong: C and F are adjacent to D; D is opposite to A, not B.

entries.question: Eight people sit in a circle facing the center. How many seats away (in either direction) is a person sitting directly opposite to another person?
entries.trick: Opposite position in an N-person circle = N / 2 steps away.
entries.why: For 8 evenly spaced people around a circle, the person directly opposite is exactly 8 / 2 = 4 seats away in either clockwise or counter-clockwise direction.
entries.why_others_wrong: 3 seats away is for a 6-person circle; 5 seats away is 3 steps in reverse; 2 seats away is 90 degrees.

entries.question: Five people A, B, C, D, E are seated around a circular table facing the center in clockwise order A, B, C, D, E. Who is sitting 2nd to the left of A?

entries.why: When facing the center, a person's left hand points in the clockwise direction. Starting from A, 1st to the left is B, and 2nd to the left is C.
entries.why_others_wrong: E is 1st to the right of A (counter-clockwise); D is 2nd to the right of A; B is 1st to the left of A.

entries.why: Standing at 12 o'clock facing the center (looking down towards 6 o'clock), your right hand points towards 10 o'clock (counter-clockwise). 1st to right is 10 o'clock, 2nd to right is 8 o'clock. So P is at 8 o'clock.
entries.why_others_wrong: 4 o'clock position comes from moving clockwise (confusing right with clockwise motion); 2 o'clock is 1st to left; 10 o'clock is 1st to right.

entries.question: Four students K, L, M, N sit in a line ordered K, L, M, N from West to East facing South. Who is to the immediate left of M?

entries.why: The seats from West to East are K(1), L(2), M(3), N(4). Since they face South, moving to someone's Left means moving Eastward (towards N). So immediate left of M is N.

entries.question: Five seats (1 to 5 from West to East) are occupied by people facing South. D is at seat 2. B sits 2nd to the left of D. Which seat is B at?

entries.question: In a row of 7 seats (1 to 7 from left to right) facing North, exactly 3 people sit between A and B. If A is at seat 2, what seat is B at?
entries.trick: 'N people between X and Y' means Y's position = X's position + (N + 1).
entries.why: If 3 people sit between A (seat 2) and B, the seats between them are seats 3, 4, and 5. Therefore, B must be at seat 6 (since 2 + (3 + 1) = 6).

entries.question: Four people sit in a row facing South. B is to the immediate right of C. D is to the immediate left of B. Who is at the leftmost position on the diagram (West end)?
entries.trick: Facing South: Right = West (left on page), Left = East (right on page).
entries.why: Facing South: 'B is right of C' puts B to the West of C (B C). 'D is left of B' puts D to the East of B (B D C). So from West to East the arrangement is B, D, C (and A). Thus B is at the West end (leftmost on diagram).

entries.question: Eight people sit in a row of 8 seats (1 to 8 left to right) facing North. P sits at seat 4. Q sits 3rd to the right of P. How many people sit to the right of Q?
entries.trick: Find Q's position: Position(P) + 3. Then calculate remaining seats to the right: Total - Position(Q).
entries.why: P is at seat 4 facing North. 3rd to the right of P is seat 4 + 3 = seat 7 (Q is at seat 7). Total seats = 8. Seats to the right of seat 7 is seat 8 only, which is 1 person.
entries.why_others_wrong: 2 people assumes Q is at seat 6; 3 people counts seats between P and Q; 0 assumes Q is at seat 8.

entries.question: Seven people sit in a row of seats 1 to 7 (left to right) facing North. C sits at seat 4 (middle). A and B sit at extreme ends. D sits 2nd to the left of C. If B is at seat 7 (right end), how many people sit between D and B?

entries.why: C is at seat 4. D sits 2nd to the left of C => seat 4 - 2 = seat 2. B is at seat 7. The seats strictly between D (seat 2) and B (seat 7) are seats 3, 4, 5, and 6. That is exactly 4 people.

entries.question: In a class of 50 students, 30 play cricket, 25 play football, and 10 play both sports. How many students play at least one of the two sports?
entries.trick: Apply Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion: n(C U F) = n(C) + n(F) - n(C intersect F).
entries.why: n(C U F) = 30 + 25 - 10 = 45 students.
entries.why_others_wrong: 55 comes from simply adding 30 + 25 without subtracting the 10 who were double-counted; 35 comes from subtracting 10 twice; 50 is the total class size.

entries.question: In a survey of 100 people, 65 drink tea and 45 drink coffee. If everyone drinks at least one beverage, how many people drink BOTH tea and coffee?
entries.trick: Rearrange Inclusion-Exclusion: n(T intersect C) = n(T) + n(C) - n(T U C).
entries.why: n(T intersect C) = 65 + 45 - 100 = 110 - 100 = 10 people.
entries.why_others_wrong: 20 comes from 65 - 45; 15 and 5 are arbitrary calculation errors.

entries.knot_name: Double-counting the intersection when finding union or complement
entries.question: In a town, 60% of people read Newspaper A, 50% read Newspaper B, and 20% read both. What percentage of people read NEITHER newspaper?
entries.trick: Find at least one newspaper reader first: n(A U B) = 60 + 50 - 20 = 90%. Neither = 100% - 90% = 10%.
entries.why: Union n(A U B) = 60% + 50% - 20% = 90%. Complement (neither) = 100% - 90% = 10%.
entries.why_others_wrong: 30% comes from calculating only A (40%) + only B (30%) = 70% and doing 100% - 70% = 30% (forgetting the 20% both readers); 20% is the intersection size; 0% comes from naively adding 60% + 50% = 110%.
entries.knot: Learners often calculate 'only A' (40%) and 'only B' (30%) and add them to get 70%, then report 100% - 70% = 30% by leaving out the 20% who read both from the union.
entries.trap_explanation: Failing to include the 20% intersection in the union leads to n(Union) = 70%, making the complement appear to be 100% - 70% = 30%.

entries.knot_name: Confusing total set size with 'only' subset size
entries.question: In a group of 80 students, 45 like Mathematics and 35 like Science. If 15 like BOTH subjects, how many students like ONLY Mathematics?
entries.trick: n(Math ONLY) = n(Math) - n(Math intersect Science) = 45 - 15 = 30.
entries.why: 45 includes students who like Math & Science. Subtracting the 15 overlap gives 45 - 15 = 30 students who like ONLY Mathematics.
entries.why_others_wrong: 45 is the total number who like Mathematics (including those who like Science); 20 is the number who like ONLY Science (35 - 15); 15 is the intersection.
entries.knot: Students frequently confuse the total count of a set n(A) with the count of elements exclusive to that set n(A only).
entries.trap_explanation: Picking 45 directly fails to subtract the 15 students who also like Science, missing the restriction 'ONLY Mathematics'.

entries.knot_name: Failing to account for the complement when applying Inclusion-Exclusion
entries.question: Out of 120 employees, 70 speak English, 50 speak French, and 20 speak neither language. How many employees speak ONLY English?
entries.trick: At least one language = 120 - 20 = 100. Both = 70 + 50 - 100 = 20. ONLY English = 70 - 20 = 50.
entries.why_others_wrong: 70 is total English speakers; 30 comes from subtracting 20 twice; 20 is the count of both or neither.
entries.knot: A common mistake is using 120 instead of 100 as the union size, which distorts the calculated intersection.
entries.trap_explanation: Setting 70 + 50 - 120 = 0 (assuming union is total 120) yields 0 both-speakers, leading to 70 ONLY English, which ignores the 20 who speak neither.

entries.knot_name: Forgetting to add back the three-set intersection in 3-set Inclusion-Exclusion
entries.question: In a class of 100 students, 50 study Math, 40 study Physics, and 30 study Chemistry. 15 study Math & Physics, 10 study Physics & Chemistry, 12 study Math & Chemistry, and 5 study all three. How many students study AT LEAST ONE subject?
entries.trick: 3-Set Formula: n(A U B U C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - [n(A intersect B) + n(B intersect C) + n(A intersect C)] + n(A intersect B intersect C).
entries.why_others_wrong: 83 comes from forgetting to add back +5 for all three; 78 comes from subtracting 5 instead of adding; 93 comes from arithmetic error.
entries.knot: Learners often forget that subtracting the pairwise intersections subtracts the center 3-set region three times, so it must be added back once (+5).
entries.trap_explanation: Calculating 120 - 37 = 83 forgets to add back the 3-set intersection +5 at the end of the 3-set Inclusion-Exclusion formula.

entries.knot_name: Failing to isolate 'exactly one' sub-regions from overlapping two-set intersections
entries.question: Using the same 3-set data (Math: 50, Physics: 40, Chem: 30; M&P: 15, P&C: 10, M&C: 12; All 3: 5), how many students study EXACTLY ONE subject?
entries.trick: Isolate single-subject regions: Math only = 50 - (10 + 7 + 5) = 28. Physics only = 40 - (10 + 5 + 5) = 20. Chem only = 30 - (7 + 5 + 5) = 13. Sum = 61.
entries.why: Pairwise only: M&P only = 10, P&C only = 5, M&C only = 7. Math only = 50 - 10 - 7 - 5 = 28. Physics only = 40 - 10 - 5 - 5 = 20. Chem only = 30 - 7 - 5 - 5 = 13. Total exactly one = 28 + 20 + 13 = 61.
entries.why_others_wrong: 46 comes from naively subtracting full pairwise intersections without adjusting for 3-set overlap: (50-15-12) + (40-15-10) + (30-12-10) = 23 + 15 + 8 = 46; 66 and 56 are miscalculations.
entries.knot: A common mistake when finding 'exactly one' is subtracting raw two-set intersections from set totals without subtracting the 3-set intersection first.
entries.trap_explanation: Subtracting full pairwise intersections (15, 10, 12) from set totals over-subtracts the center region, yielding 23 + 15 + 8 = 46.

entries.trap_explanation: Flat SI = 15000×20×2/100 = 6000 ignores that the second year's 20% growth should apply to 18000 (the amount after year 1), not the original 15000 — a genuine but incomplete calculation.

entries.question: The compound interest on a certain sum for 2 years at 10% per annum is ₹1050. Find the sum.

entries.knot_name: Given principal, amount & time, find the compound rate
entries.question: A sum of ₹4000 amounts to ₹4840 in 2 years at compound interest, compounded annually. Find the rate of interest per annum.
entries.trick: Amount = P(1+R/100)^T, so (1+R/100) = (Amount/P)^(1/T).
entries.why_others_wrong: 21% is the total CI-to-principal ratio ((4840−4000)/4000×100=21%), mistaken for the annual rate without taking the square root; 10.5% and 20% come from other partial-step slips.
entries.knot: The learner computes the OVERALL 2-year growth percentage (21%) correctly but stops there, without taking the square root to find the per-year compound rate — 21% is a real, correctly-derived number, just for the wrong quantity.
entries.trap_explanation: Computing (4840−4000)/4000×100 = 21% gives the total growth over both years, not the annual rate — a rushed learner may report this directly since it's a genuine, correctly-computed percentage from the problem's own numbers.

**Mistakenly applying the flat SI formula to a compound-interest question**

Amount = 20000 × (1.05)² = 20000 × 1.1025 = 22050. CI = 22050 − 20000 = 2050. Shortcut / Key Trick: Amount = P(1+R/100)^T; CI grows on an increasing base each year, unlike SI which stays flat. Common Trap (T1): Computing flat SI = 20000×5×2/100 = 2000 applies the rate to the original (unchanged) base every year instead of the growing base that compound interest requires — a subtly wrong but very close-looking answer.

**Core Intuition for Mistakenly applying the flat SI formula to a compound-interest question**

Simple Interest is calculated on the original principal every period — it stays flat. Compound Interest is calculated on the growing balance (principal + accumulated interest) each period — it grows faster every year. For the same rate and time, CI always exceeds SI. The test: does last period's interest get added to the balance before this period's interest is computed?

entries.question: A car covers 180 km in 4 hours. Find its speed.
entries.trick: Speed = Distance ÷ Time.
entries.why: Speed = 180/4 = 45 km/hr.
entries.why_others_wrong: 40, 50, and 36 come from small arithmetic slips in the division.

entries.knot_name: Converting km/hr to m/s (or vice versa) — using the wrong conversion factor or direction
entries.question: Convert 72 km/hr into m/s.
entries.trick: To convert km/hr to m/s, multiply by 5/18.
entries.why_others_wrong: 259.2 m/s wrongly multiplies by 18/5 instead of 5/18 (using the conversion factor for the OPPOSITE direction); 40 m/s and 13.33 m/s come from other misapplied factors.
entries.knot: There are two conversion factors (5/18 and 18/5) depending on direction, and it's easy to grab the wrong one, especially under time pressure — multiplying by 18/5 when converting km/hr→m/s inflates the answer dramatically.
entries.trap_explanation: Multiplying by 18/5 instead of 5/18 (72×18/5=259.2) applies the conversion factor meant for m/s→km/hr to a km/hr→m/s conversion, using the reciprocal of the correct factor.

entries.knot_name: Converting km/hr to m/s (or vice versa) — using the wrong conversion factor or direction
entries.question: Convert 15 m/s into km/hr.
entries.trick: To convert m/s to km/hr, multiply by 18/5.
entries.why_others_wrong: 4.17 km/hr wrongly multiplies by 5/18 instead of 18/5 (opposite-direction factor); 27 and 60 come from other misapplied conversions.
entries.knot: Same knot in the reverse direction — using 5/18 instead of 18/5.
entries.trap_explanation: Multiplying by 5/18 instead of 18/5 (15×5/18≈4.17) applies the km/hr→m/s factor to an m/s→km/hr conversion, using the reciprocal of the correct factor.

entries.knot_name: Converting km/hr to m/s (or vice versa) — using the wrong conversion factor or direction
entries.question: Convert 108 km/hr into m/s.
entries.trick: Multiply km/hr by 5/18 to get m/s.
entries.why_others_wrong: 388.8 m/s wrongly multiplies by 18/5; 60 and 21.6 come from other misapplied factors.
entries.knot: Same recurring conversion-direction knot.
entries.trap_explanation: Multiplying by 18/5 instead of 5/18 (108×18/5=388.8) inflates the value using the reciprocal factor.

entries.knot_name: Average speed for two equal-distance legs at different speeds — must use 2ab/(a+b), not the arithmetic mean
entries.question: A car travels from city X to city Y at 40 km/hr and returns from Y to X (the same distance) at 60 km/hr. Find the average speed for the entire trip.
entries.trick: For two legs of EQUAL distance at different speeds, average speed = (2×speed1×speed2) ÷ (speed1+speed2) — NOT the simple average of the two speeds.
entries.why_others_wrong: 50 km/hr wrongly averages the two speeds directly ((40+60)/2=50); 45 km/hr and 100 km/hr come from other miscalculations.
entries.knot: Since the car spends MORE time at the slower speed (covering the same distance), the true average speed is weighted toward the slower speed — but a simple average of the two speeds (50) looks like the obvious, clean answer.
entries.trap_explanation: Averaging the two speeds directly — (40+60)/2=50 km/hr — ignores that more time is spent traveling at the slower speed, which pulls the true average below the simple midpoint.

entries.knot_name: Average speed for two equal-distance legs at different speeds — must use 2ab/(a+b), not the arithmetic mean
entries.question: A cyclist rides to a destination at 30 km/hr and returns via the same route at 50 km/hr. Find the average speed for the whole journey.
entries.trick: Average speed = (2×speed1×speed2)/(speed1+speed2) for equal-distance legs.
entries.why_others_wrong: 40 km/hr wrongly averages the two speeds directly; 35 and 60 come from other miscalculations.
entries.knot: Same knot — the naive average (40) looks plausible but ignores the extra time spent at the slower speed.
entries.trap_explanation: Averaging the two speeds directly ((30+50)/2=40 km/hr) overestimates the true average since more time is spent at the slower 30 km/hr speed.

entries.knot_name: Relative speed: ADD speeds when moving in opposite directions, SUBTRACT when moving in the same direction — mixing these up flips the answer
entries.question: Two trains of lengths 120 m and 80 m are running on parallel tracks in the SAME direction at 54 km/hr and 36 km/hr respectively. Find the time taken by the faster train to completely cross the slower one.
entries.trick: For trains moving in the SAME direction, relative speed = difference of their speeds. Time to cross = (sum of lengths) ÷ (relative speed, converted to consistent units).
entries.why: Relative speed = 54−36=18 km/hr = 18×5/18=5 m/s. Total length = 120+80=200 m. Time = 200/5 = 40 seconds.
entries.why_others_wrong: 8 seconds wrongly uses the SUM of speeds (as if moving in opposite directions) instead of the difference; 22.2 seconds and 80 seconds come from other miscalculations or unit errors.
entries.knot: Since both trains are moving in the SAME direction, their relative speed is the DIFFERENCE (the faster train only gains ground slowly on the slower one) — but the more commonly drilled 'crossing' scenario (trains moving toward each other) uses SUM, and this habit can carry over incorrectly.
entries.trap_explanation: Using the sum of speeds (54+36=90 km/hr=25 m/s) instead of the difference treats the same-direction scenario as if the trains were moving toward each other, giving Time=200/25=8 seconds — the wrong direction of relative motion.

entries.knot_name: Relative speed: ADD speeds when moving in opposite directions, SUBTRACT when moving in the same direction — mixing these up flips the answer
entries.question: The same two trains (120 m and 80 m long, speeds 54 km/hr and 36 km/hr) are now running on parallel tracks in OPPOSITE directions. Find the time taken for them to completely cross each other.
entries.trick: For trains moving in OPPOSITE directions, relative speed = sum of their speeds.
entries.why: Relative speed = 54+36=90 km/hr = 90×5/18=25 m/s. Total length=200 m. Time = 200/25 = 8 seconds.
entries.why_others_wrong: 40 seconds wrongly uses the DIFFERENCE of speeds (as if moving in the same direction) instead of the sum; 22.2 seconds and 4 seconds come from other miscalculations.
entries.knot: The mirror-image knot of the previous one — here using the difference instead of the sum is the trap.
entries.trap_explanation: Using the difference of speeds (54−36=18 km/hr=5 m/s) instead of the sum treats the opposite-direction scenario as if the trains were moving the same way, giving Time=200/5=40 seconds — the wrong direction of relative motion.

entries.knot_name: Crossing a stationary pole/person needs only the train's OWN length; crossing a platform/bridge needs train length PLUS platform length
entries.question: A train 120 m long, running at 36 km/hr, crosses a platform 180 m long. Find the time taken to completely cross the platform.
entries.trick: When crossing a platform, the train must cover its OWN length PLUS the platform's length. Time = (train length + platform length) ÷ speed.
entries.why: Speed = 36 km/hr = 36×5/18=10 m/s. Total distance = 120+180=300 m. Time = 300/10 = 30 seconds.
entries.why_others_wrong: 12 seconds wrongly uses ONLY the train's length (as if crossing a pole, not a platform), forgetting to add the platform's length; 18 seconds and 8.57 seconds come from other miscalculations.
entries.knot: Crossing a POLE only requires the train's own length (since a pole has no length of its own), but crossing a PLATFORM requires adding the platform's length too — it's easy to forget this addition and treat every 'crossing' scenario the same way as crossing a pole.
entries.trap_explanation: Using only the train's length (120m) and computing Time=120/10=12 seconds silently drops the platform's length from the calculation, as if the train were crossing a point object rather than an extended platform.

entries.knot_name: Crossing a stationary pole/person needs only the train's OWN length; crossing a platform/bridge needs train length PLUS platform length
entries.question: A train 150 m long, running at 54 km/hr, crosses a platform 150 m long. Find the time taken to completely cross the platform.
entries.trick: Time = (train length + platform length) ÷ speed.
entries.why: Speed = 54×5/18=15 m/s. Total distance = 150+150=300 m. Time = 300/15 = 20 seconds.
entries.why_others_wrong: 10 seconds wrongly uses only the train's length, ignoring the platform; 15 and 5.56 seconds come from other miscalculations.
entries.knot: Same knot — forgetting to add the platform's length to the train's own length.
entries.trap_explanation: Using only the train's length (150m), Time=150/15=10 seconds, silently drops the platform's contribution to the total distance covered.

entries.question: In a 100 m race, A finishes in 10 seconds and beats B by 20 meters. Find B's speed.
entries.trick: 'A beats B by 20 m' means that when A completes the full 100 m, B has covered only 100−20=80 m in that same 10 seconds. Use this to find B's speed.
entries.why: When A finishes (100m in 10s), B has covered 100−20=80 m. B's speed = 80/10 = 8 m/s.
entries.why_others_wrong: 10 m/s wrongly assumes B ran the FULL 100m in the same 10 seconds, ignoring the 20m deficit entirely; 2 m/s wrongly treats the 20m AS B's total distance covered; 12 m/s comes from an unrelated miscalculation.
entries.knot: 'Beats by 20 meters' is easy to misread as 'B is 20 meters ahead of where he'd need to be' or to simply ignore, computing B's speed as if B also covered the full 100m distance in the same time as A — but the correct reading is that B is 20m SHORT of the finish line when A crosses it.
entries.trap_explanation: Computing B's speed as 100/10=10 m/s (the same as if B ran the full 100m in 10 seconds, identical to A) completely ignores the stated 20m deficit, treating A and B as tied instead of A winning by that margin.

entries.question: In a 200 m race, A finishes in 20 seconds and beats B by 40 meters. Find the time B takes to complete the full 200 m race.
entries.trick: When A finishes (200m in 20s), B has covered 200−40=160m. Find B's speed from this, then compute B's time for the full 200m.
entries.why: B's distance when A finishes = 200−40=160m. B's speed = 160/20=8 m/s. B's time for 200m = 200/8=25 seconds.
entries.why_others_wrong: 20 seconds wrongly assumes B finishes at the same time as A, ignoring the deficit; 16 and 24 seconds come from other miscalculations.
entries.knot: Same knot — properly interpreting 'beats by 40 meters' as B's shortfall at the moment A finishes, then extrapolating B's own finishing time.
entries.trap_explanation: Assuming B also finishes in 20 seconds (the same as A) ignores that A specifically 'beat' B, meaning B was still running (40m short) when A crossed the line.

entries.knot_name: Journey covered partly at one speed and partly at another — given total distance & total time, find the distance covered at EACH speed (not the total split evenly)
entries.question: A man travels a total of 16 km, partly on foot at 4 km/hr and partly by bicycle at 12 km/hr, taking a total of 2 hours. Find the distance he covered on foot.
entries.trick: Let the foot-distance be d. Set up d/4 + (16−d)/12 = 2 (time for each segment, summed to the total time) and solve for d.
entries.why_others_wrong: 8 km wrongly assumes the distance is split evenly (16/2=8) between the two modes; 12 km and 6 km come from incorrect algebraic setups.
entries.knot: It's tempting to assume the total distance is split evenly (half by foot, half by bicycle) since only ONE total distance and ONE total time are given — but the actual split depends on the two different speeds and must be solved for algebraically, not assumed.
entries.trap_explanation: Assuming an even 8 km/8 km split (since only aggregate totals are given) ignores that the two speeds are different, meaning the actual time spent on each segment — and hence the correct distance split — is NOT equal.

72 × 5/18 = 360/18 = 20 m/s. Shortcut / Key Trick: To convert km/hr to m/s, multiply by 5/18. entries.content:
**Average speed for two equal-distance legs at different speeds — must use 2ab/(a+b), not the arithmetic mean**

Average speed = (2×40×60)/(40+60) = 4800/100 = 48 km/hr. Shortcut / Key Trick: For two legs of EQUAL distance at different speeds, average speed = (2×speed1×speed2) ÷ (speed1+speed2) — NOT the simple average of the two speeds. Core Knot: Since the car spends MORE time at the slower speed (covering the same distance), the true average speed is weighted toward the slower speed — but a simple average of the two speeds (50) looks like the obvious, clean answer. Common Trap (T5): Averaging the two speeds directly — (40+60)/2=50 km/hr — ignores that more time is spent traveling at the slower speed, which pulls the true average below the simple midpoint.

**Core Intuition for Average speed for two equal-distance legs at different speeds — must use 2ab/(a+b), not the arithmetic mean**

50 km/hr wrongly averages the two speeds directly ((40+60)/2=50); 45 km/hr and 100 km/hr come from other miscalculations.

entries.content:
**Relative speed: ADD speeds when moving in opposite directions, SUBTRACT when moving in the same direction — mixing these up flips the answer**

Relative speed = 54−36=18 km/hr = 18×5/18=5 m/s. Total length = 120+80=200 m. Time = 200/5 = 40 seconds. Shortcut / Key Trick: For trains moving in the SAME direction, relative speed = difference of their speeds. Time to cross = (sum of lengths) ÷ (relative speed, converted to consistent units). Core Knot: Since both trains are moving in the SAME direction, their relative speed is the DIFFERENCE (the faster train only gains ground slowly on the slower one) — but the more commonly drilled 'crossing' scenario (trains moving toward each other) uses SUM, and this habit can carry over incorrectly. Common Trap (T3): Using the sum of speeds (54+36=90 km/hr=25 m/s) instead of the difference treats the same-direction scenario as if the trains were moving toward each other, giving Time=200/25=8 seconds — the wrong direction of relative motion.

**Core Intuition for Relative speed: ADD speeds when moving in opposite directions, SUBTRACT when moving in the same direction — mixing these up flips the answer**

8 seconds wrongly uses the SUM of speeds (as if moving in opposite directions) instead of the difference; 22.2 seconds and 80 seconds come from other miscalculations or unit errors.

entries.content:
**Crossing a stationary pole/person needs only the train's OWN length; crossing a platform/bridge needs train length PLUS platform length**

Speed = 36 km/hr = 36×5/18=10 m/s. Total distance = 120+180=300 m. Time = 300/10 = 30 seconds. Shortcut / Key Trick: When crossing a platform, the train must cover its OWN length PLUS the platform's length. Time = (train length + platform length) ÷ speed. Core Knot: Crossing a POLE only requires the train's own length (since a pole has no length of its own), but crossing a PLATFORM requires adding the platform's length too — it's easy to forget this addition and treat every 'crossing' scenario the same way as crossing a pole. Common Trap (T7): Using only the train's length (120m) and computing Time=120/10=12 seconds silently drops the platform's length from the calculation, as if the train were crossing a point object rather than an extended platform.

**Core Intuition for Crossing a stationary pole/person needs only the train's OWN length; crossing a platform/bridge needs train length PLUS platform length**

12 seconds wrongly uses ONLY the train's length (as if crossing a pole, not a platform), forgetting to add the platform's length; 18 seconds and 8.57 seconds come from other miscalculations.

entries.question: Simplify the expression: (2³ × 2⁴)² ÷ 2⁵.
entries.trick: Apply index laws in order: a^m × a^n = a^(m+n), (a^m)^n = a^(m×n), and a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m-n).
entries.why: Inside parentheses: 2³ × 2⁴ = 2³⁺⁴ = 2⁷. Raising to power 2: (2⁷)² = 2⁷ˣ² = 2¹⁴. Dividing by 2⁵: 2¹⁴ ÷ 2⁵ = 2¹⁴⁻⁵ = 2⁹ = 512.
entries.why_others_wrong: 256 is 2⁸ (from 2¹³ ÷ 2⁵); 1024 is 2¹⁰ (from adding exponents in power-of-power); 128 is 2⁷.

entries.question: Rationalize the denominator of 10 / √5 and simplify.
entries.trick: Multiply numerator and denominator by √5.
entries.why_others_wrong: 5√5 comes from dividing 10 by 2 instead of 5; 10√5 misses dividing by the denominator 5; 2 ignores the surd term √5 completely.

entries.knot_name: Confusing power-of-a-power with product-of-powers
entries.question: Simplify (x³)⁴ × x².
entries.trick: Use (x^m)^n = x^(m×n) first, then x^a × x^b = x^(a+b).
entries.why: (x³)⁴ = x³ˣ⁴ = x¹². Then x¹² × x² = x¹²⁺² = x¹⁴.
entries.why_others_wrong: x⁹ comes from adding exponents in (x³)⁴ to get x⁷, then x⁷ × x² = x⁹; x²⁴ comes from multiplying all exponents (3 × 4 × 2); x¹⁰ comes from x³⁺⁴⁺³.
entries.knot: Adding exponents when raising a power to a power (thinking (x^m)^n = x^(m+n) instead of x^(m×n)).
entries.trap_explanation: x⁹ traps students who write (x³)⁴ as x⁷ (adding 3+4) and then add 2 to get x⁹.

entries.knot_name: Misinterpreting negative fractional exponent as negative result
entries.question: Evaluate 27^(-2/3).
entries.trick: Negative exponent means reciprocal: a^(-m/n) = 1 / (a^(1/n))^m.
entries.why_others_wrong: -9 results from making the evaluated number negative due to the minus sign in the exponent; 9 misses the negative sign reciprocal effect; -1/9 combines both errors.
entries.knot: Treating a negative exponent as making the overall result a negative number rather than taking the reciprocal.
entries.trap_explanation: -9 traps students who assume a negative sign in an exponent negates the answer instead of reciprocating it.

entries.knot_name: Rationalization with wrong conjugate or forgetting denominator difference
entries.question: Rationalize the denominator of 6 / (√5 - √2) and simplify.
entries.trick: Multiply top and bottom by conjugate (√5 + √2) and divide by difference of squares (5 - 2 = 3).
entries.why_others_wrong: 2√5 - 2√2 uses wrong conjugate sign; 6√5 + 6√2 forgets to divide by denominator difference (5 - 2 = 3); 3√5 + 3√2 divides by 2 instead of 3.
entries.knot: Forgetting to divide by (a - b) in the denominator after multiplying the numerator by the conjugate.
entries.trap_explanation: 6√5 + 6√2 traps students who multiply the numerator by conjugate but forget that (√5)² - (√2)² = 3 in the denominator.

entries.knot_name: Forgetting to rationalize before algebraic substitution
entries.question: If x = 1 / (2 - √3), find the value of x + (1 / x).
entries.trick: Rationalize x first: x = (2 + √3) / (4 - 3) = 2 + √3. Then 1/x = 2 - √3.
entries.why_others_wrong: 2√3 comes from subtracting integer parts instead of adding; 4 + 2√3 comes from adding x twice; 2 comes from halving the answer.
entries.knot: Trying to manipulate unrationalized fractions in expressions like x + 1/x, leading to sign and surd calculation errors.
entries.trap_explanation: 2√3 traps students who mess up signs while adding (2 + √3) and (2 - √3), cancelling 2 instead of √3.

entries.knot_name: Failing to distribute exponent multiplier across all terms
entries.question: Solve for x: 9^(x + 1) = 27^(x - 1).
entries.trick: Express both bases as powers of 3: (3²)^(x+1) = (3³)^(x-1), then equate exponents 2(x+1) = 3(x-1).
entries.why_others_wrong: 2 comes from failing to distribute 2 and 3 to constant terms (writing 2x + 1 = 3x - 1 => x = 2); 3 and 4 come from arithmetic errors in balancing linear equation.
entries.knot: Writing (3²)^(x+1) as 3^(2x+1) instead of 3^(2x+2), forgetting to multiply the exponent base power to all terms inside the parenthetical exponent.
entries.trap_explanation: 2 traps students who multiply only the variable x by the base exponent (writing 2x + 1 = 3x - 1) instead of distributing to both terms.

entries.knot_name: Misapplying square root to additive surd terms sqrt(a+b)
entries.question: Find the square root of 7 + 4√3.
entries.trick: Express 7 + 4√3 in the form (a + b) + 2√(ab) = (√a + √b)².
entries.why: 7 + 4√3 = 7 + 2√12. We need two numbers with sum = 7 and product = 12, which are 4 and 3. So √(7 + 4√3) = √4 + √3 = 2 + √3.
entries.why_others_wrong: 4 + √3 comes from taking sqrt of 7 wrongly; 1 + 2√3 yields (1+2√3)² = 13 + 4√3; 3 + √2 yields (3+√2)² = 11 + 6√2.
entries.knot: Assuming sqrt(7 + 4√3) can be evaluated by taking square root of 7 and 4√3 separately.
entries.trap_explanation: 4 + √3 traps students who try to take square roots term-by-term (sqrt(16)+sqrt(3) etc.) instead of expressing as a perfect square (√a + √b)².

**Misapplying square root to additive surd terms sqrt(a+b)**

7 + 4√3 = 7 + 2√12. We need two numbers with sum = 7 and product = 12, which are 4 and 3. So √(7 + 4√3) = √4 + √3 = 2 + √3. Shortcut / Key Trick: Express 7 + 4√3 in the form (a + b) + 2√(ab) = (√a + √b)². Core Knot: Assuming sqrt(7 + 4√3) can be evaluated by taking square root of 7 and 4√3 separately. Common Trap (T1): 4 + √3 traps students who try to take square roots term-by-term (sqrt(16)+sqrt(3) etc.) instead of expressing as a perfect square (√a + √b)².

**Core Intuition for Misapplying square root to additive surd terms sqrt(a+b)**

The square root of a sum is not the sum of the square roots: √(a+b) ≠ √a + √b. For example, √(9+16) = √25 = 5, but √9 + √16 = 3 + 4 = 7. When simplifying √(p + q√r), assume the answer has the form a + b√r, square it, match coefficients, and solve for a and b. Never split the root across an addition or subtraction sign.

entries.question:
Statements: All cats are mammals. All mammals are animals.
Conclusions:
I. All cats are animals.
II. Some animals are cats.
entries.trick: In universal affirmative statements (All A are B, All B are C), transitive inclusion (All A are C) holds, and conversion to 'Some C are A' is always valid.
entries.why: Cats ⊆ Mammals ⊆ Animals. Therefore, all cats are inside the Animals set (I follows). Since the set of cats is a non-empty subset of animals, at least some animals are cats (II follows).
entries.why_others_wrong: Only I or Only II misses one of the valid inferences; Neither follows ignores basic set inclusion.

entries.question:
Statements: No circle is a square. All squares are triangles.
Conclusions:
I. Some triangles are squares.
II. No circle is a triangle.
entries.trick: Draw the minimum-overlap Venn diagram: 'All squares are triangles' guarantees 'Some triangles are squares'. But circles can overlap triangles outside squares.
entries.why: Since all squares are inside triangles, at least the part of triangles occupied by squares makes 'Some triangles are squares' definitely true (I follows). Circles are disjoint from squares, but circles may or may not overlap the non-square part of triangles, so II does not definitely follow.
entries.why_others_wrong: Only II or Both follow incorrectly assumes circles cannot overlap triangles; Neither follows overlooks that 'All A are B' implies 'Some B are A'.

entries.knot_name: Confusing 'Some' with 'All' or assuming transitivity in 'Some' relations
entries.question:
Statements: Some pens are pencils. Some pencils are erasers.
Conclusions:
I. Some pens are erasers.
II. All erasers are pencils.
entries.trick: 'Some A are B' and 'Some B are C' does not yield any definite relation between A and C. 'Some B are C' does not imply 'All C are B'.
entries.why: The overlap between pens and pencils may be completely separate from the overlap between pencils and erasers, so I is not definite. 'Some pencils are erasers' only guarantees partial overlap, not that all erasers are pencils, so II is not definite.
entries.why_others_wrong: Only I, Only II, and Both follow all assume non-existent definite connections from partial 'Some' premises.
entries.knot: Assuming that 'Some' statements chain transitively or imply 'All' statement conversions.
entries.trap_explanation: Learners often treat 'Some A are B' and 'Some B are C' like 'All A are B' and 'All B are C', falsely concluding 'Some A are C'.

entries.knot_name: Confusing 'Some' with 'All' or assuming transitivity in 'Some' relations
entries.question:
Statements: All apples are fruits. Some fruits are sweet.
Conclusions:
I. Some apples are sweet.
II. All sweet items are fruits.
entries.trick: The subset 'sweet' intersects 'fruits', but not necessarily the 'apples' sub-region of fruits. 'Some A are B' never converts to 'All B are A'.
entries.why: Apples are a subset of fruits. 'Some fruits are sweet' does not force the 'sweet' region to overlap with 'apples', so I does not follow definitely. 'Some fruits are sweet' does not mean all sweet things are fruits (e.g., sugar is sweet), so II does not follow.
entries.why_others_wrong: Only I assumes mandatory overlap between apples and sweet fruits; Only II mistakes 'Some' for 'All'.
entries.knot: Confusing partial overlap of a larger set ('fruits') with guaranteed overlap of its subset ('apples').
entries.trap_explanation: Assuming a property of 'some elements of the larger container' automatically applies to the 'smaller container inside it'.

entries.knot_name: Confusing possible conclusions with definite conclusions
entries.question:
Statements: All doctors are scientists. Some scientists are artists.
Conclusions:
I. Some doctors being artists is a possibility.
II. Some doctors are artists.
entries.trick: A conclusion stating 'is a possibility' is TRUE if at least one valid Venn diagram supports it without violating premises. A definite statement requires ALL valid Venn diagrams to support it.
entries.why: Doctors ⊆ Scientists. Scientists and Artists overlap. A Venn diagram where Artists overlap the Doctor portion of Scientists is valid and violates no premise, so possibility (I) holds. However, Artists can overlap Scientists without touching Doctors, so definite claim (II) does not hold.
entries.why_others_wrong: Only II or Both follow mistake a possible overlap for a mandatory definite overlap.
entries.knot: Treating 'is a possibility' as false just because it is not definitely true, or treating 'is definitely true' and 'is possible' as identical.
entries.trap_explanation: Failing to distinguish between possibility statements (needs 1 valid diagram) and definite statements (needs all valid diagrams).

entries.knot_name: Confusing possible conclusions with definite conclusions
entries.question:
Statements: Some books are papers. No paper is a pen.
Conclusions:
I. Some books are not pens.
II. All books being pens is a possibility.
entries.trick: The books that are papers CANNOT be pens. This makes 'Some books are not pens' DEFINITELY TRUE, which in turn makes 'All books being pens' IMPOSSIBLE.
entries.why: Since 'Some books are papers' and 'No paper is a pen', those specific books that are papers can never be pens. Thus, 'Some books are not pens' is definitely true (I follows). Since at least those books cannot be pens, it is impossible for all books to be pens, so II does not follow.
entries.why_others_wrong: Only II and Both follow fail to recognize that 'No paper is a pen' strictly blocks the books-that-are-papers from ever becoming pens.
entries.knot: Overlooking negative premises when evaluating possibilities.
entries.trap_explanation: Assuming 'anything is possible' in possibility questions without checking if a negative premise creates an absolute barrier.

entries.question:
Statements: All A are B. All B are C. No C is D.
Conclusions:
I. No A is D.
II. Some B are A.
entries.trick: Nested inclusion: A ⊆ B ⊆ C. Since C is completely separated from D, A (inside C) is also completely separated from D.
entries.why: Since A is inside B and B is inside C, and no C is D, A is also entirely disjoint from D (No A is D follows). Also, since All A are B (and set A is non-empty), those B that are A guarantee 'Some B are A' follows.
entries.why_others_wrong: Only I or Only II misses one of the two completely valid deductions.

entries.question:
Statements: Some cars are buses. Some buses are trains.
Conclusions:
I. Some cars are trains.
II. No car is a train.
entries.trick: Check for complementary pair criteria: Same subject & predicate ('cars' and 'trains'), both conclusions individually uncertain, one affirmative ('Some') and one negative ('No').
entries.why: Neither conclusion is individually definite from the given statements. However, in logic, cars and trains must either share at least one element (Some cars are trains) OR share zero elements (No car is a train). Exactly one of these two complementary conditions must hold.
entries.why_others_wrong: Neither follows ignores the complementary 'Either/Or' relation between affirmative and negative statements on the same terms.

entries.question: A can do a piece of work in 10 days and B can do it in 15 days. In how many days will they finish the work together?
entries.trick: Add individual rates: 1/10 + 1/15 = 5/30 = 1/6. Invert to get 6 days.
entries.why: Combined rate = sum of individual rates. A's rate = 1/10, B's rate = 1/15. Together = 1/6 per day, so 6 days total.
entries.why_others_wrong: 5 days assumes simple addition of speeds; 8 days underestimates combined effort; 12 days is close to B alone.

entries.knot_name: Wage Division by Efficiency
entries.question: A and B together earn ₹2700 in 9 days. A alone can do the work in 15 days and B in 45 days. What is B's share?
entries.trick: Efficiency ratio A:B = 1/15 : 1/45 = 3:1. B's share = (1/4) × 2700 = ₹675.
entries.why: Wages are divided in the ratio of efficiencies (work done per day). A does 3 parts while B does 1 part.
entries.why_others_wrong: ₹900 assumes equal split; ₹1350 is A's actual share; ₹1800 reverses the ratio.
entries.knot: Wages in time-and-work are always divided in ratio of efficiencies (reciprocal of days).
entries.trap_explanation: Students often divide wages equally or reverse who gets the larger share.

entries.knot_name: Wage Division by Efficiency
entries.question: A, B and C can do a job in 10, 12 and 15 days. They get ₹3000 for the job. What is A's share?
entries.why: LCM of 10,12,15 = 60. A does 6 units/day, B does 5, C does 4. Total 15 units. A's share = 6/15 × 3000.
entries.why_others_wrong: ₹1000 is equal split; ₹800 is C's share; ₹1500 over-credits A.
entries.knot: Wages in time-and-work are always divided in ratio of efficiencies (reciprocal of days).
entries.trap_explanation: The trap is assuming equal division instead of proportional to efficiency.

entries.knot_name: Men-Days Inverse Proportion
entries.question: If 12 men can finish a job in 20 days, how many days will 15 men take to finish the same job?
entries.trick: Men × Days = constant. 12 × 20 = 15 × D → D = 240/15 = 16 days.
entries.why: Total work = 12 × 20 = 240 man-days. With 15 men, days = 240/15 = 16.
entries.why_others_wrong: 18 is a miscalculation; 24 assumes direct proportion; 25 adds instead of dividing.
entries.knot: Men-Days product is constant when total work is fixed (inverse proportion).
entries.trap_explanation: Students often use direct proportion (more men = more days) instead of inverse.

entries.knot_name: Workers Leave Partway Through
entries.question: A can do a work in 12 days. B can do it in 18 days. A starts alone. After 4 days B joins. In how many more days will the work be finished?
entries.trick: A does 4/12 = 1/3 alone in 4 days. Remaining = 2/3. Together they do 1/12+1/18 = 5/36 per day. 2/3 ÷ 5/36 = 24/5 ≈ 5 days.
entries.why: After A works 4 days: work left = 1 - 1/3 = 2/3. Combined rate = 5/36. Time = (2/3)/(5/36) = 24/5 = 4.8 ≈ 5 days.
entries.why_others_wrong: 4 days underestimates remaining work; 6 days ignores A's solo contribution; 8 days is too high.
entries.knot: When workers join or leave midway, split the problem into phases.
entries.trap_explanation: The trap is forgetting to account for work already done in the first phase.

entries.knot_name: Workers Leave Partway Through
entries.question: A and B together can do a work in 12 days. A alone can do it in 20 days. After working together for 4 days, A leaves. In how many days will B finish the remaining work?
entries.trick: B's rate = 1/12 - 1/20 = 2/60 = 1/30. After 4 days together: done = 4/12 = 1/3. Remaining = 2/3. B alone: (2/3)/(1/30) = 20 days.
entries.why: Combined rate 1/12. A's rate 1/20. B's rate = 1/12 - 1/20 = 1/30. Work done in 4 days = 4×1/12 = 1/3. Remaining 2/3 at rate 1/30 = 20 days.
entries.why_others_wrong: 16 miscalculates B's rate; 24 assumes B works at combined rate; 30 is B's total time alone.
entries.knot: When workers join or leave midway, split the problem into phases.
entries.trap_explanation: Students confuse B's individual rate with the combined rate.

entries.knot_name: Men-Women Mixed Rate
entries.question: 3 men and 4 women can do a work in 6 days. 5 men and 2 women can do the same work in 4 days. In how many days can 1 man and 1 woman do the work?
entries.trick: Let 1 man's rate = m, 1 woman's rate = w. (3m+4w)×6 = 1, (5m+2w)×4 = 1. Solve: m=1/30, w=1/120. Together = 1/30+1/120 = 5/120 = 1/24. Answer: 24 days.
entries.why: From equation 1: 18m + 24w = 1. From equation 2: 20m + 8w = 1. Solving gives m=1/30, w=1/120. Combined rate = 1/24.
entries.why_others_wrong: 18 days confuses the setup; 20 miscalculates; 36 assumes very slow combined work.
entries.knot: When men and women have different rates, set up simultaneous equations.
entries.trap_explanation: The trap is treating men and women as having equal efficiency.

Total work = 12 × 20 = 240 man-days. With 15 men, days = 240/15 = 16. Shortcut / Key Trick: Men × Days = constant. 12 × 20 = 15 × D → D = 240/15 = 16 days. Core Knot: Men-Days product is constant when total work is fixed (inverse proportion). Common Trap (direct-vs-inverse): Students often use direct proportion (more men = more days) instead of inverse.

**Core Intuition for Men-Days Inverse Proportion**

More workers means fewer days (inverse proportion): Workers × Days = constant (the total work in man-days). If 8 men finish in 12 days, total work = 96 man-days. For 6 men: days = 96 ÷ 6 = 16. For 12 men: days = 96 ÷ 12 = 8. Compute total man-days first; never assume more workers means more days.

**Workers Leave Partway Through**

After A works 4 days: work left = 1 - 1/3 = 2/3. Combined rate = 5/36. Time = (2/3)/(5/36) = 24/5 = 4.8 ≈ 5 days. Shortcut / Key Trick: A does 4/12 = 1/3 alone in 4 days. Remaining = 2/3. Together they do 1/12+1/18 = 5/36 per day. 2/3 ÷ 5/36 = 24/5 ≈ 5 days. Core Knot: When workers join or leave midway, split the problem into phases. Common Trap (phase-splitting): The trap is forgetting to account for work already done in the first phase.

**Core Intuition for Workers Leave Partway Through**

Split the work into phases at the point where someone leaves. Phase 1: all workers together until the departure. Phase 2: remaining workers alone. Compute work done in Phase 1 (combined rate × time), subtract from the total job (= 1), then find how long the remaining workers need to finish the remainder at their own combined rate.

entries.question: A train 150 meters long is running at a speed of 54 km/hr. How much time will it take to pass a stationary telegraph pole?
entries.trick: Convert speed to m/s by multiplying by 5/18, then Time = Train Length ÷ Speed.
entries.why: Speed in m/s = 54 × (5/18) = 15 m/s. Since a pole has negligible width, total distance covered is the train length (150 m). Time = 150 ÷ 15 = 10 seconds.
entries.why_others_wrong: 12, 15, and 8 seconds result from calculation errors like dividing 150 by 12.5 or using the wrong unit conversion factor.

entries.question: A 200 m long train crosses a platform 300 m long in 25 seconds. Find the speed of the train in km/hr.
entries.trick: Total Distance = Train Length + Platform Length. Speed (km/hr) = (Distance ÷ Time) × (18/5).
entries.why: Total distance = 200 + 300 = 500 m. Speed in m/s = 500 ÷ 25 = 20 m/s. Converting to km/hr gives 20 × (18/5) = 72 km/hr.
entries.why_others_wrong: 43.2 km/hr uses platform length alone (300/25 × 18/5); 28.8 km/hr uses train length alone (200/25 × 18/5); 90 km/hr is an arithmetic error.

entries.question: A train traveling at 90 km/hr crosses a bridge of length 400 m in 24 seconds. What is the length of the train?
entries.trick: Total distance covered = Speed × Time. Train length = Total distance − Bridge length.
entries.why: Speed in m/s = 90 × (5/18) = 25 m/s. Total distance covered in 24 seconds = 25 × 24 = 600 m. Train length = 600 − 400 = 200 m.
entries.why_others_wrong: 600 m is the total distance covered without subtracting bridge length; 400 m is just the bridge length; 250 m is a calculation mistake.

entries.question: A train 150 m long crosses a pole in 15 seconds. Find its speed in km/hr.
entries.trick: Speed = Distance/Time. Distance is train length (150 m), time is 15 s. Convert m/s to km/hr by ×18/5.
entries.why_others_wrong: 30 and 40 come from arithmetic slips in the m/s to km/hr conversion; 45 overshoots by misapplying the conversion factor.
entries.trap_explanation: Skipping or misapplying the m/s↔km/hr conversion factor (×18/5 or ×5/18) is the base-level trap even in the clean case.

entries.content: A train crossing any stationary point (pole, man standing still) only needs to cover its own length. So Distance = length of train. Time is given. Speed = Distance/Time gives m/s; multiply by 18/5 to get km/hr, or given km/hr multiply by 5/18 to get m/s. This single relationship — Rate × Time = Quantity — is the backbone of every train problem; the complexity added later is always about what the correct 'distance' or 'combined speed' should be, not this core formula.

Think of the train as a long snake. To fully pass a pole, the tail must also cross the pole — so the snake has to slide forward by its own body length. If the snake is 10 m long and takes 2 seconds to fully pass, it moved 10 m in 2 s, i.e. 5 m every second. That's the speed.

entries.addresses: Why is the distance equal to the train's length and not something else, since a pole has no length?
entries.content: Distance covered = movement of the front minus movement needed for the back to also clear the point. Since the pole is a single point (zero length), the train must move exactly its own length for the entire train to pass it.

entries.question: A train 200 m long running at 72 km/hr crosses a platform in 30 seconds. Find the length of the platform.

entries.why_others_wrong: 600 m is the trap — stopping after computing total distance without subtracting the train's own length. 300 m and 500 m come from arithmetic or conversion slips.
entries.knot: Learner treats platform length as the total distance crossed, forgetting the train's own body must also be added to what needs to be covered.
entries.trap_explanation: 600 m is a genuine correct intermediate value (total distance covered) that looks like a complete answer, tempting the learner to stop before subtracting the train length.

entries.content: When a train crosses a platform (or bridge), the distance covered equals the train's length PLUS the platform's length — because the train isn't 'done' crossing until its tail clears the far end of the platform, and the front had to travel the full platform length before that. So: Distance = Speed × Time = Train Length + Platform Length. Whichever of these three is unknown, solve for it after computing total distance.

Imagine a 5 m toy train and a 10 m platform drawn on the floor. The train's front starts at the platform's start. For the train to be fully off the platform, the BACK of the train must reach the platform's end. The front therefore travels: platform length (10 m) + train's own length (5 m) = 15 m total. Nothing more, nothing less.

entries.addresses: Why do we add the platform length AND the train length instead of just the platform length?
entries.content: The platform length alone only tells you how far the FRONT needs to travel to reach the far edge. But the question asks when the train has fully crossed — meaning the tail is also past the platform. That extra distance the tail needs to cover is exactly the train's own length.

entries.knot_name: Same-Direction Crossing (Relative Speed = Difference)
entries.question: Two trains 120 m and 180 m long run on parallel tracks in the same direction at 60 km/hr and 42 km/hr. How long will they take to cross each other?
entries.trick: Same direction → relative speed = difference of speeds. Distance to cover = sum of lengths. Time = Distance/Relative Speed.
entries.why: Relative speed = 60-42=18 km/hr = 5 m/s. Distance = 120+180=300 m. Time = 300/5 = 60 s.
entries.why_others_wrong: 50, 40, 30 s come from wrongly adding the speeds (as if opposite direction) or conversion slips.
entries.knot: Learner defaults to adding the two speeds regardless of direction, applying the opposite-direction rule to a same-direction scenario.
entries.trap_explanation: The correct move (subtract speeds) is the reverse of the more commonly drilled opposite-direction case (add speeds) — direction reversal trap.

entries.content: When two trains move in the SAME direction, the faster one only gains on the slower one at the rate of their speed DIFFERENCE — think of chasing a slower car; you close the gap based on how much faster you are, not your combined speed. So relative speed = |Speed A - Speed B|. When moving in OPPOSITE directions, they approach each other at the SUM of their speeds instead. Distance to cover while crossing = sum of both train lengths in either case. Time = Distance/Relative Speed.

Picture yourself jogging at 6 km/hr behind a friend jogging at 5 km/hr, same direction. You're only gaining on them at 1 km/hr — the difference — even though you're both moving fast. Now picture walking toward each other on a corridor: your speeds add up because you're closing the gap from both sides at once. Trains work exactly the same way.

entries.addresses: Why does the distance to cover still equal the sum of both lengths, even though they're moving the same direction?
entries.content: Regardless of direction, 'crossing' means the two trains go from just-touching-front to fully-separated-at-the-back. That relative displacement is always the sum of both lengths — only the RATE at which that displacement happens (relative speed) changes with direction.

entries.why_others_wrong: 30 km/hr comes from treating 14.4 as the answer directly or a conversion slip. 33.6 and 42 come from using only one train's length as distance, or arithmetic errors.
entries.knot: Learner uses only one train's length (120 m instead of 240 m) as the distance to be covered, forgetting both trains' lengths contribute to the full pass.
entries.trap_explanation: Using a single train length gives a plausible but incomplete distance figure, mirroring the platform-length partial-application trap in a new costume.

entries.knot_name: Opposite-Direction Crossing (Relative Speed = Sum)
entries.question: Two trains 110 m and 90 m long run on parallel tracks towards each other at 60 km/hr and 40 km/hr. Find the time they take to cross each other.
entries.trick: Opposite directions → relative speed = sum of speeds. Distance = sum of lengths. Time = Distance/Relative Speed.
entries.why_others_wrong: 10, 8, 6 s come from using only one train's length, or subtracting speeds instead of adding.
entries.knot: Learner subtracts the speeds (applying the same-direction rule here) or uses only one train's length as distance.
entries.trap_explanation: Direction-reversal trap: subtracting speeds is correct for same-direction, not opposite-direction, motion.

entries.content: When two trains move TOWARD each other, they close the gap using their COMBINED speed — each contributes its full speed to shrinking the distance between them. So relative speed = Speed A + Speed B. Distance to cover for a full crossing = sum of both lengths, same as always. Time = Distance/Relative Speed.

Two people walking toward each other, one at 3 km/hr and one at 2 km/hr, close a gap between them at 5 km/hr combined — much faster than either alone. That's because both are eating into the same gap from opposite ends simultaneously. Trains passing each other on parallel tracks work the same way.

entries.addresses: How do I remember which case adds speeds and which subtracts?
entries.content: Opposite directions = 'toward each other' = gap shrinks from both sides = ADD. Same direction = 'chasing' = gap shrinks only by the speed difference = SUBTRACT. Tie it to the everyday image: walking toward a friend vs. jogging behind one.

entries.knot_name: Opposite-Direction Crossing (Relative Speed = Sum)
entries.question: A train 160 m long crosses a man running in the opposite direction at 6 km/hr in 6 seconds. Find the train's speed.
entries.trick: Relative speed = train speed + man's speed (opposite directions, man treated as a point). Distance = train length only.
entries.why: Relative speed=160/6=26.67 m/s=96 km/hr. Train speed=96-6=90 km/hr.
entries.why_others_wrong: 96 km/hr is the trap — the relative speed reported as the train's own speed, forgetting to subtract the man's contribution. 84 and 102 come from sign errors.
entries.knot: Learner correctly finds the relative speed but reports it directly instead of subtracting the man's speed to isolate the train's actual speed.
entries.trap_explanation: 96 km/hr is a genuine correct intermediate value (the relative speed) that looks complete on its own.

entries.knot_name: Tunnel/Bridge with 'Completely Inside' Phrasing
entries.question: A train 150 m long moving at 54 km/hr enters a tunnel 850 m long. For how long is the train completely inside the tunnel (fully hidden)?
entries.trick: 'Completely inside' means distance = Tunnel length - Train length (not +), since the train is fully hidden only between the point where its tail enters and its front exits.
entries.why: Speed=54 km/hr=15 m/s. Distance = 850-150=700 m. Time=700/15=46.67 s.
entries.why_others_wrong: 66.67 s comes from wrongly adding lengths (850+150) as in the standard crossing case. 60 and 50 s come from arithmetic slips.
entries.knot: Learner defaults to the standard 'sum of lengths' rule (used for fully crossing a platform) instead of recognizing that 'completely inside/hidden' requires SUBTRACTING the train length from the tunnel length.
entries.trap_explanation: Direction-reversal on the arithmetic operation: the heavily-drilled 'add lengths' rule for full crossing is wrongly reused here, when the phrasing actually demands subtraction.

entries.content: 'Completely inside/hidden' is a different question from 'completely crossed.' The train is fully hidden starting when its TAIL enters the tunnel, and stops being fully hidden the moment its FRONT exits. The front travels the full tunnel length to exit; but the 'fully hidden' phase only starts once the tail has already gone in — which happens after the front has already travelled the train's own length. So the fully-hidden distance = Tunnel Length − Train Length, the opposite operation from the standard crossing case.

Picture a 3 m toy train and a 10 m tunnel drawn on the floor. The train is 'fully hidden' only from the moment its back end disappears into the tunnel mouth, until its front end pokes back out the far side. The front has to travel the whole 10 m to exit, but by the time the tail goes in, the front has already gone 3 m in. So the 'fully hidden' stretch is only 10-3=7 m, not 10 m and definitely not 13 m.

entries.addresses: Why subtract here when every other train problem tells me to add the lengths?
entries.content: Adding lengths answers 'how long to fully CROSS' (front enters to tail exits). Subtracting answers a narrower question: 'how long is it fully INSIDE/hidden' (tail enters to front exits) — a shorter middle portion of the same journey. Same setup, different question, different arithmetic.

entries.knot_name: Tunnel/Bridge with 'Completely Inside' Phrasing
entries.question: A train moving at 90 km/hr is completely inside a 600 m tunnel for exactly 16 seconds. Find the length of the train.
entries.trick: Distance for hidden phase = Speed×Time = Tunnel length - Train length. Rearrange to find train length.
entries.why: Speed=90 km/hr=25 m/s. Distance=25×16=400 m. Train length=Tunnel-Distance=600-400=200 m.
entries.why_others_wrong: 400 m is the trap — mistaking the computed 'hidden distance' itself for the train length. 250 and 150 m come from arithmetic slips.
entries.knot: Learner computes the hidden-phase distance correctly but reports it directly as the train length instead of subtracting it from the tunnel length.
entries.trap_explanation: 400 m is a genuine, correct intermediate value that looks complete on its own, tempting an early stop before the final subtraction.

entries.knot_name: Tunnel/Bridge with 'Completely Inside' Phrasing
entries.question: A train is completely inside a 480 m tunnel for 10 seconds, and completely crosses the same tunnel (front-entry to tail-exit) in 30 seconds. Find the train's length.
entries.trick: Crossing distance = Tunnel + Train; Hidden distance = Tunnel - Train. Same speed in both, so equate S from both equations and solve for train length L.
entries.why_others_wrong: 300 m comes from swapping which equation uses + and -. 180 and 120 m come from arithmetic slips in solving the linear equation.
entries.knot: Learner sets up the two equations but swaps which one gets the + and which gets the -, or makes an algebraic slip while eliminating speed.
entries.trap_explanation: Combining the two timing-based relationships (crossing vs. hidden) without correctly relating them through a shared, correctly-signed speed variable.

entries.knot_name: Converting Relative Speed Before vs. After Combining
entries.question: Two trains, one 270 m long running at 120 km/hr and the other 230 m long running at 80 km/hr, run in opposite directions on parallel tracks. In what time will they cross each other?
entries.trick: Combine speeds first in km/hr (120+80=200), THEN convert the combined speed to m/s, then divide distance by it.
entries.why: Relative speed=200 km/hr=500/9 m/s. Distance=270+230=500 m. Time=500÷(500/9)=9 s.
entries.why_others_wrong: 10, 7.2, 12 s come from converting each speed to m/s separately first and making rounding/arithmetic errors, or from adding already-converted approximate values.
entries.knot: Learner converts each speed to m/s separately (introducing rounding errors) instead of combining in km/hr first and converting once, or mismatches units between distance (m) and speed at some intermediate step.
entries.trap_explanation: Unit-mismatch trap: doing the unit conversion at the wrong stage, or converting piecewise, introduces rounding drift that produces a close-but-wrong answer.

entries.content: When combining (adding or subtracting) two speeds given in km/hr, do the combination FIRST while still in km/hr — it's exact, whole-number arithmetic. Only convert to m/s AFTER you have the single combined relative speed. Converting each speed separately first (especially with non-round numbers) invites rounding errors that compound. One clean conversion beats two messy ones.

If you owe a friend 120 rupees and another friend 80 rupees, you'd add them as 200 rupees total, then convert to dollars once at the end — not convert each debt to dollars separately (with rounding each time) and then add the rounded dollar figures. Same logic: add/subtract speeds in their original clean unit first, convert once at the end.

entries.addresses: Does converting each speed separately always give a wrong final answer, or just sometimes?
entries.content: Mathematically both orders give the same exact answer if you keep full fractions throughout. The trap only bites when you round intermediate m/s values (e.g. rounding 120 km/hr to '33.3 m/s' instead of keeping 100/3). Combining in km/hr first avoids the temptation to round early.

entries.content: Rate × Time = Quantity problems in the trains costume can feel like they multiply into a dozen unrelated rules, but they're really one relationship applied to different 'what counts as distance' situations. It's okay if this hasn't clicked yet — try switching to a different pattern for now and come back to this one later with fresh eyes; the same idea often lands better on a second pass.

If the numeric walkthroughs aren't landing, try picturing the whole thing physically instead: draw a straight line, mark the train as a thick segment on it, and physically trace how far the FRONT of that segment moves for each scenario (pole, platform, tunnel, another train). Once the picture is right, the arithmetic is just Distance/Time. No rush — this is a common sticking point, not a sign you're behind.

This knot has tripped up plenty of learners on the first pass — that's expected, not a red flag. Consider parking Trains for today and revisiting Speed-Distance-Time basics or Boats & Streams instead, since they share the same core relative-speed idea in a simpler setting; coming back to Trains afterward is often much easier.

entries.why_others_wrong: 140 cm² forgets to multiply by 1/2; 35 cm² divides by 4 instead of 2; 84 cm² comes from multiplying base by 6 instead of height.

entries.knot_name: Using hypotenuse as a leg in Pythagoras theorem
entries.question: A right-angled triangle has a hypotenuse of length 13 cm and one leg of length 5 cm. What is the length of the other leg?
entries.trick: In Pythagoras theorem (a² + b² = c²), the hypotenuse c is the longest side. To find a missing leg, subtract: leg = √(c² − a²).
entries.why_others_wrong: 13.9 cm comes from adding 13² + 5² = 194 (√194 ≈ 13.9); 18 cm comes from 13 + 5; 8 cm comes from 13 − 5 without squaring.
entries.knot: Learners often automatically add the squares of the two given numbers (a² + b²) regardless of whether one of them is the hypotenuse.
entries.trap_explanation: Applying c = √(a² + b²) when c (hypotenuse) is already given produces √(169 + 25) = √194 ≈ 13.9 cm, which mistakenly treats the hypotenuse as a second leg.

entries.knot_name: Using hypotenuse as a leg in Pythagoras theorem
entries.question: A 15-meter ladder is placed against a wall so that it reaches a window 12 meters above the ground. How far is the foot of the ladder from the base of the wall?
entries.trick: The ladder acts as the hypotenuse (15 m). Distance from wall = √(ladder² − height²) = √(15² − 12²).
entries.why_others_wrong: 19.2 m comes from adding squares √(15² + 12²) = √369 ≈ 19.2 m; 27 m comes from 15 + 12; 3 m comes from 15 − 12 without squaring.
entries.knot: Treating the ladder (hypotenuse) and height (leg) both as legs, adding their squares instead of subtracting.
entries.trap_explanation: Adding 15² + 12² = 369 gives √369 ≈ 19.2 m, which is impossible because a leg cannot be longer than the ladder itself.

entries.knot_name: Confusing side ratio with area ratio in similar triangles
entries.question: Two similar triangles have corresponding sides in the ratio 3 : 5. If the area of the smaller triangle is 36 cm², what is the area of the larger triangle?
entries.trick: For similar figures, Area Ratio = (Side Ratio)². Here Area Ratio = (3/5)² = 9/25.
entries.why_others_wrong: 60 cm² applies the linear side ratio directly (36 × 5/3 = 60); 120 cm² doubles the linear calculation; 80 cm² is an arbitrary estimate.
entries.knot: Learners often use the linear side ratio 3:5 directly for areas instead of squaring the ratio to 9:25.
entries.trap_explanation: Multiplying area by (5/3) gives 60 cm², which forgets that area is a 2D measure scaling with the square of the linear dimensions.

entries.knot_name: Confusing side ratio with area ratio in similar triangles
entries.question: Triangle ABC is similar to Triangle DEF. The ratio of area(ABC) to area(DEF) is 16 : 49. If side AB = 12 cm, what is the length of the corresponding side DE?
entries.trick: Side Ratio = √(Area Ratio). Side Ratio = √(16/49) = 4/7.
entries.why_others_wrong: 36.75 cm uses area ratio directly (12 × 49/16); 14.7 cm multiplies 12 by 49/40; 28 cm miscalculates the square root ratio.
entries.knot: Multiplying the side length directly by the area ratio 49/16 without taking the square root first.
entries.trap_explanation: Computing 12 × (49/16) = 36.75 cm directly applies area ratio to a 1D length, overlooking the square-root relationship.

entries.knot_name: Using hypotenuse as a leg in Pythagoras theorem
entries.question: An isosceles triangle has two equal sides of length 10 cm each and a base of length 12 cm. Calculate the area of the triangle.
entries.trick: Draw the altitude to the base. It bisects the base into two 6 cm segments. Height = √(10² − 6²) = √(100 − 36) = √64 = 8 cm.
entries.why: Height = √(100 − 36) = 8 cm. Area = (1/2) × base × height = (1/2) × 12 × 8 = 48 cm².
entries.why_others_wrong: 60 cm² multiplies base by slant side directly ((1/2) × 12 × 10); 24 cm² uses half-base in area formula; 96 cm² forgets to divide by 2.
entries.knot: Using the slant side (10 cm) directly as height, or using the full base 12 in the right triangle calculation.
entries.trap_explanation: Taking (1/2) × 12 × 10 = 60 cm² assumes the slant side of 10 cm is perpendicular to the base, which is false.

entries.knot_name: Confusing side ratio with area ratio in similar triangles
entries.question: In triangle ABC, a line segment PQ parallel to base BC divides the triangle into a smaller top triangle APQ of area 25 cm² and a trapezium PBCQ of area 24 cm². What is the ratio of segment PQ to base BC?
entries.trick: Total area of triangle ABC = Area(APQ) + Area(PBCQ) = 25 + 24 = 49 cm². Ratio of areas = 25 : 49. Ratio of sides = √(25/49) = 5 : 7.
entries.why: Area(APQ)/Area(ABC) = 25/49. Since APQ ~ ABC, PQ/BC = √(25/49) = 5/7.
entries.why_others_wrong: 25 : 49 gives the area ratio instead of side ratio; 5 : 24 compares side to trapezium area square root; 25 : 24 directly compares the two areas.
entries.knot: Comparing area of top triangle directly to area of trapezium instead of full triangle area, or forgetting to take the square root.
entries.trap_explanation: Using 25:49 directly forgets to take the square root for 1D lengths, while using 25:24 compares top area to trapezium area rather than full triangle area.

entries.question: A ladder 10 m long leans against a vertical wall, making an angle of 60° with the ground. How high up the wall does the ladder reach?
